# FAQ

We know you'll have plenty of questions throughout the semester, and we're here to help. This page aims to answer some of the most common questions, but it won't provide a solution to every problem you might encounter.

By third year, you should have developed a substantial toolkit of ecological knowledge, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills. One of the goals of this assignment is to give you the opportunity to apply those skills to a real ecological study with the freedom to make decisions about your own analyses and research questions.

There won't always be a single "correct" answer, and that's intentional. Ecological research often involves navigating uncertainty, justifying decisions, and evaluating alternative approaches. We encourage you to discuss ideas within your group, consult the literature, and think critically before seeking guidance.

Of course, you are not on your own. If you become stuck, are unsure whether you're heading in the right direction, or simply want to discuss your ideas, please reach out to us. We are happy to help, provide feedback, and point you in the right direction. Our role is not to give you all the answers, but to help you develop the confidence and skills to find them yourself.

If we think you're heading down a path that is unlikely to answer your research question or meet the project objectives, we'll give you a nudge to help get you back on track. Otherwise, don't be afraid to explore ideas, try different approaches, and learn from the process. After all, that is the essence of the scientific process.

## Where can we find what species are in the area?

There are many only resources at your disposal where you can find information about species occurrences. Have a think back to previous units.

We will go through how to make a species list in BirdNET, but it would be best to have a basic understanding of who may be in the region and how they respond to fire (and why) before your Week 4 presentation.

## Why not record continuously?

Recorders sample the first 10 minutes of each hour rather than recording continuously. Ideally we would record continuously, however, this would reduce the total duration of the study to less than 1 week. We also record bats on the same devices, and as these devices cannot record acoustic (birds) and ultrasonic (bats) at the same time, we must compromise.

Our approach greatly increases deployment duration while still providing representative samples of bird activity throughout the day. Recent studies suggest that even sampling across the day can provide reliable metrics of bird diversity and activity.

## There are NAs in our combined dataset or the metadata is in the wrong column. Why, and what should I do?

This is likely caused by the folder structure not being as the code expects. For example, the device folder is missing between the site and date folders. As a result, the code will continue to use the folder path as it's written to, resulting in data being in the wrong columns and NAs in the dataset as well.

Another reason is if one of the site numbers in the folder structure is incorrect, such as `UB8_06` being spelled as `ub8_06`, `UB8_6`, `Ub8_06`, or `UB_06`. The code expects `UB8_06` and R is case-specific. If one of your sites is spelled incorrectly in the folder structure, the code will fail to assign a treatment and will result in `NA`, which will make it very difficult to do your analyses.

## What should be included in the Methods section of my report?

Have a look at the current literature and the answers are all there for you. Some of the key details that are common throughout ecoacoustic and fire ecology papers - but unique to this study design - can be found throughout this repository. The rest is up to you to determine, ask about, or figure out.
